title: How to House a Construction Crew of 6: A Practical Guide
meta_description: What to check when housing a crew of 6 away from home: location, parking, costs, paperwork and a simple booking checklist.
excerpt: A practical guide for project managers housing a crew of 6 away from home, from choosing the right house to parking and paperwork.
body_markdown:
Housing a crew of 6 away from home comes down to four things: one base for the whole team, a short drive to site, enough parking, and a price that covers everything. A whole house usually beats hotel rooms on all four, as long as you book it properly and early.

> **Key takeaways**
> - Keep the crew together in one house where you can, with a bedroom each.
> - Check the drive time to site at your actual start time, not the middle of the day.
> - Confirm parking for every van and trailer before you book.
> - Ask for one price per person per night with bills, Wi-Fi and cleaning included.
> - Agree how you will extend or shorten the booking if the programme moves.

## Why a whole house works for a crew of 6

Hotels are built for single travellers. When you put a crew of 6 into a hotel, you pay for 6 rooms, 6 breakfasts and often 6 parking spaces, and your team spends every evening eating out. It also splits the crew up, which makes early starts harder to organise.

A whole house gives the team one base. Everyone has their own bedroom, there is a kitchen for cooking proper meals, and there is a living room where people can switch off after a shift. Supervisors find it easier to brief a team that is in one place, and lift-sharing to site is simple when everyone leaves from the same door.

### What to look for in the house

- **A bedroom for each person.** Sharing rooms on a long job leads to poor sleep and short tempers.
- **Enough bathrooms.** For a crew of 6, two bathrooms make a real difference at 5am.
- **A proper kitchen.** A cooker, fridge freezer and space to prepare packed lunches.
- **A washing machine.** Work clothes need washing more than once a week.
- **Good Wi-Fi.** For timesheets, calls home and evening paperwork.

## Getting the location right

The best house is not always the closest one. Think about how your crew will travel and when.

### Measure the real drive

Check the drive time at your actual start and finish times. A route that takes a few minutes at lunchtime can take much longer at shift change when a large site empties. If your crew works nights, check that the house is quiet enough to sleep in during the day.

### Think about the whole programme

If the job moves along a route, such as a road or rail scheme, pick a base that works for the first months and plan a move later if needed. It is usually cheaper and less disruptive than moving the crew every few weeks.

### Check local services

Crews appreciate being near a supermarket, a takeaway and somewhere to fill up with fuel. On remote sites, a small town base is often better than a village with nothing open after 6pm.

## Parking, vans and kit

Parking causes more problems on working-away jobs than anything else. Before you book, write down:

- How many vans and cars the crew will bring.
- Whether any vans tow trailers or plant.
- Whether any vans are too high for multi-storey or covered parking.
- Whether you need to store tools or materials securely overnight.

Then ask the accommodation provider to confirm, in writing, how many vehicles the house can take. Never assume on-street parking will be available, especially in towns with permit schemes.

## Budgeting for the stay

The cleanest way to budget is a single price per person per night that already includes everything. With StaysDirect, bills, Wi-Fi, council tax and cleaning are part of the price, so you are not chasing meter readings or utility accounts.

### Costs people forget

- **Parking charges** at hotels and in town centres.
- **Laundry** if there is no washing machine.
- **Meals out** every night when there is no kitchen.
- **Admin time** spent booking and managing lots of separate rooms.

A whole house removes most of these. Our crews typically find a house works out 30 to 50% cheaper than hotels once everything is counted, but always compare like for like on your own job.

### Travel and subsistence

If you pay travel and subsistence to your team, keep clear records of where they stay, for how long, and what you pay directly. The rules on what is allowable depend on the circumstances of each worker and job. Read the [HMRC guidance on travel and subsistence](https://www.gov.uk/guidance/travel-mileage-and-fuel-rates-and-allowances) and talk to your payroll team. Check current HMRC guidance before relying on this.

## Booking and paperwork

When you ask for a quote, send the same information every time so you can compare providers fairly:

- Crew size and any mix of trades or supervisors.
- Site postcode.
- Start date and expected length of stay.
- Vehicles and parking needs.
- Who will be the contact for the crew on site.

Ask about payment terms. Many operators, including StaysDirect, offer weekly and monthly terms, and approved business accounts can pay on 14 to 30 day credit terms. That keeps accommodation in line with how you pay other suppliers.

### Handling changes

Programmes move. Agree up front how much notice you need to give to extend or end a booking, and whether you can add a second house if the crew grows. A direct operator can usually make these changes faster than an agency, because there is no middle layer to go through.

It also helps to name one person on your side who can approve changes. When a programme slips, the accommodation provider needs a quick yes or no on extending, and a single contact avoids crews turning up to a house that has been released. Keep that contact in the booking notes so the support team knows who to call.

## A simple checklist

Before your crew travels, check that you have:

- Confirmed the address, key collection and arrival time.
- Sent the crew the house rules, Wi-Fi details and the support phone number.
- Confirmed parking for every vehicle.
- Agreed the end date and how to extend.
- Saved the support number for problems out of hours.

faqs.question: Is a house cheaper than a hotel for a crew of 6?
faqs.answer: Usually, yes. You pay for one house instead of separate rooms, and a kitchen cuts the cost of eating out. Always compare like for like on your own job.

faqs.question: How many bedrooms does a crew of 6 need?
faqs.answer: Ideally one bedroom each. Sharing rooms on long jobs affects sleep and morale.

faqs.question: What should be included in the price?
faqs.answer: Look for bills, Wi-Fi, council tax and cleaning in one price per person per night, so there are no surprises.

faqs.question: How far in advance should I book?
faqs.answer: As early as you have firm dates. Areas near large projects fill up, so book as soon as the programme is confirmed and agree how to extend.

faqs.question: Can I pay on account?
faqs.answer: Many operators offer credit terms. StaysDirect offers 14 to 30 day credit terms for approved business accounts.
